name: Part 2 — Practice
tagline: Sixty-six cue cards, one minute to plan, two minutes to fill
blurb: The complete Quarter 3 cue-card bank sorted by family, the narrative language that long turns actually run on, the tense system that carries them, and three model answers to compare against — after you have recorded your own.
modelQ: Describe a time when you were stuck in a traffic jam for a very long time
modelType: The EVENT family — setting, complication, reaction, resolution, reflection.

vocab.g: PERSON cards — character shown through behaviour
items: Be naturally good at something, often social.
She has a knack for making people feel at ease within about thirty seconds of meeting them.
go out of your way to
Make a special effort for someone. The best phrase for the helps others cards.
He went out of his way to find me a second-hand copy, and then refused to let me pay for it.
Resemble an older relative in character, not appearance.
Everyone says I take after my grandmother, which I've decided to treat as a compliment.
He was never one to give advice, which is exactly why I listened when he finally did.
She put the whole room at ease simply by admitting she had no idea what she was doing either.
Transfer by influence, usually a quality.
That calmness of hers rubbed off on the entire team within a couple of weeks.

vocab.g: PLACE cards — sensory and spatial detail
items: Hidden and hard to find, with a pleasant sense of discovery.
It's a tiny place tucked away behind the market, and you'd walk past it three times before finding it.
Extremely crowded. British, informal, perfect for the crowded-place card.
By eight in the evening the whole street was heaving and you couldn't move without apologising.
Low continuous sound. Useful for making quiet audible.
The loudest thing in the room was the hum of the air conditioning, which tells you how quiet it was.
At six in the morning the whole valley was stone-cold silent, and I could hear my own footsteps.
The reading room overlooks the river, so you spend half your time not reading.
Away from the places tourists go.
It's well off the beaten track — no signs, no bus route, and that's precisely the appeal.
Cost me. Informal, usually with a large amount.
It set me back about three months' savings, which felt reckless at the time and doesn't now.
I've held on to it through four house moves, even though I've never once used it.
Something kept for the memory attached to it.
It stopped being useful years ago — it's a keepsake now, and it lives on the shelf.
Worn through heavy use. A far better detail than old.
The case is battered and the corner is cracked, and I'd be genuinely upset if I lost it.
Given how often I use it, the thing has paid for itself several times over.
Refuse to give it up. A natural closing line.
It's worth almost nothing to anyone else, but I wouldn't part with it for any money.
My heart sank the moment I saw the queue going round the corner of the building.
I suddenly understood. British and very natural in storytelling.
It was only when everyone started getting out of their cars that the penny dropped.
Stop gradually and completely. Ideal for traffic and systems.
The whole motorway ground to a halt about forty minutes outside the city.
Then, completely out of the blue, the driver announced we were going back the way we came.
Judging with knowledge gained later. A closing move.
In hindsight it was obvious, but at the time none of us saw it coming.
It threw me completely, because I'd rehearsed what I was going to say about six times.
I got into the habit of walking home instead of taking the bus, and now I miss it if I don't.
I was dreadful at it for about a year, but I stuck at it and something eventually clicked.
I've been doing it on and off since school, with two or three long gaps in between.
Occupy yourself while waiting. Central to the waste-of-time card.
It started as something to kill time on the commute and turned into an hour every evening.
with the best will in the world
However much I want to. Introduces an honest limitation.
With the best will in the world, I'm never going to be good at this — and I've made peace with that.
After three years it's become second nature; I don't decide to do it, I just do it.

vocab.g: MEDIA and ABSTRACT cards — reaction and significance
items: It struck a chord with an enormous number of people, judging by how fast it spread.
I saw it once, four years ago, and it has stuck in my mind ever since.
It got the message across in thirty seconds without a single word of dialogue.
Deal with something important too briefly.
My one complaint is that it glossed over the part I was most curious about.
It's a slow burn — I didn't think much of it at first and then couldn't stop thinking about it.
The last line hit home rather harder than I was expecting on a Tuesday evening.

grammar.intro: Part 2 is where Grammatical Range is won or lost, because a two-minute narrative either uses the tense system or flattens into past simple. These five structures are what a Band 7 long turn is built from; the six error patterns are what keeps otherwise fluent candidates at Band 6.

structures.use: Every EVENT and most PERSON cards.
structures.form: past continuous (scene) → past simple (events) → past perfect (what came before)
structures.ex: I was scrolling through my phone when the driver announced that the bridge had been closed for two hours.
structures.note: All three in one sentence is worth doing deliberately at least once. It demonstrates range faster than anything else available.

structures.n: had been -ing for duration before a past point
structures.use: Anything involving waiting, saving, or a long build-up.
structures.ex: We had been sitting in the same spot for nearly three hours by then.
structures.note: Under-used and highly visible. One instance per long turn is enough.

structures.use: Foregrounding the point of the story.
structures.form: What + clause + be …  ·  It was … that/who …
structures.ex: What really got to me was the silence in the car. / It was the driver who eventually gave up.
structures.note: A cleft is the cheapest way to show grammatical flexibility while sounding entirely natural.

structures.ex: Stuck on the bridge with no signal, I ended up talking to a stranger for an hour.
structures.note: Opening a sentence this way is a strong Band 8 signal and takes no extra words.

structures.use: Whenever another person appears in the story.
structures.ex: He said the traffic wasn't going to move before midnight, and that we should find somewhere to eat.
structures.note: Mixing one line of direct speech with one of reported speech gives you both the intonation change and the grammar.

errors.bad: I sat in the car. The radio said the bridge was closed. I waited three hours. I felt angry.
errors.good: I had been sitting there twenty minutes when the radio announced the bridge had closed. By the time it reopened I had been waiting three hours.
errors.why: Not an error of accuracy but of range, and it is what holds narratives at Band 6. The descriptor at Band 7 requires a range of structures used flexibly; a single tense cannot satisfy it.

errors.n: Past perfect used where past simple belongs
errors.bad: Then I <s>had gone</s> home and I <s>had eaten</s> dinner.
errors.good: Then I went home and had dinner.
errors.why: Past perfect marks something earlier than the main narrative, not a later event. Over-correction is as damaging as under-use and sounds stranger.

errors.bad: <s>While</s> the phone rang, I was cooking. / <s>When</s> I was waiting, the message arrived.
errors.good: While I was cooking, the phone rang. / When the message arrived, I was still waiting.
errors.why: While takes the longer background action; when takes the shorter interrupting one. Reversing them makes the sequence unclear.

errors.bad: I <s>am used to</s> go there every summer. / I <s>used to</s> the noise now.
errors.good: I used to go there every summer. / I'm used to the noise now.
errors.why: used to + infinitive is a past habit. be used to + noun or -ing is present familiarity. Two different structures that sound almost identical.

errors.bad: I got on <s>bus</s> and sat next to <s>old man</s> who was reading <s>newspaper</s>.
errors.good: I got on the bus and sat next to an old man who was reading a newspaper.
errors.why: Singular countable nouns always need a determiner. In a two-minute narrative this error can occur fifteen times, and at that density it becomes systematic rather than occasional.

errors.n: Time expressions in the wrong position
errors.bad: I <s>last year went</s> to Da Nang. / I go <s>usually</s> by train.
errors.good: Last year I went to Da Nang. / I usually go by train.
errors.why: Definite time expressions go at the start or the end of the clause, never between subject and verb. Frequency adverbs go before the main verb.

models.html:
I want to talk about a time when I was stuck in a traffic jam. It happened last year when I went to my hometown for Tết.

I took a bus from Hanoi. Normally the trip takes about three hours but that day there was a lot of traffic. We stopped for a long time and nobody knew why. I felt very tired and angry because I wanted to arrive before dinner.

While I waited, I listened to music and I talked to the person next to me. He was very friendly. Finally the bus moved again and I arrived at ten o'clock, five hours late.

I felt relieved but also very tired. It was a bad experience.
models.len: about 70 seconds — below the required range

notes.fc: The four prompts are answered in order and the sequence is clear. But it stops at seventy seconds, and an answer that ends before ninety has not demonstrated the ability to speak at length, which caps this criterion regardless of accuracy.
notes.lr: A lot of traffic, very tired and angry, very friendly, a bad experience. Sufficient to convey meaning, with no less common item anywhere. Very appears three times.
notes.gr: Past simple throughout, with one while clause. Accurate, but there is no past perfect, no past continuous for scene, no relative clause. This is the range limitation that defines Band 6 here.
notes.pr: Clear and intelligible. Stress falls on content words but the rhythm does not change between the tense section and the reflective section, so the story has no shape in the delivery.

models.html:
The worst one I can remember was the Tết before last, on the road out of Hanoi. I'd booked the early coach specifically to avoid the rush, which turned out to be optimistic.

We'd been moving reasonably well for about an hour when everything simply stopped. No announcement, no explanation — just four lanes of stationary vehicles as far as I could see. After twenty minutes people started getting out of their cars, which is when I realised this wasn't a normal delay.

What I remember most is how quickly strangers started talking to each other. The man beside me had been travelling the same route for fifteen years and he said, quite cheerfully, "This is nothing. Wait until tomorrow." He shared his sunflower seeds and we complained about the government for two hours.

In the end it took nine hours for a journey that should have taken three, and I got home long after everyone had gone to bed. Oddly, it's one of the Tết journeys I remember most fondly — which says something about how little the delay actually mattered.

notes.fc: The turn is sustained without noticeable effort, opens on a specific memory rather than an announcement, and closes on a reflection that was not signalled at the start. Discourse markers vary in function throughout.
notes.lr: Turned out to be optimistic, stationary vehicles, a normal delay, remember most fondly. Less common items appear naturally and the dry humour of we complained about the government for two hours shows register awareness.
notes.gr: Past perfect (I'd booked), past perfect continuous (had been travelling), a sentential relative clause, and reported detail. Error-free and genuinely varied, though a couple of sentences are still plainly constructed.
notes.pr: The quoted line is delivered in a different voice, and the pause before just four lanes of stationary vehicles creates the reveal. Stress on nine against three makes the contrast audible.

models.html:
Nine hours for a journey that takes three. And the strange part is that I'd do it again.

This was the Tết before last, heading north out of Hanoi — the one journey a year when the entire country appears to be going in the same direction as you are. I'd booked the five a.m. coach on the theory that nobody else would be mad enough, a theory the four lanes of stationary traffic disposed of by six.

We'd been stopped about forty minutes before anyone accepted it was permanent. Then the doors opened, and something quite odd happened. People got out. Not to look — to talk. Within half an hour there was a sort of impromptu village strung out along the hard shoulder, strangers sharing sunflower seeds and phone chargers as though they'd arranged it in advance.

The man next to me had done that road every Tết for fifteen years and said, more or less delighted, "This is nothing. Wait till tomorrow." Had I been alone I think I'd have been furious. As it was, I spent two hours being told the family history of a man whose name I never learned.

I got home at eleven, to a house asleep and a plate of cold bánh chưng. And what stayed with me wasn't the delay at all — it was how quickly people abandoned being annoyed once it became obvious that being annoyed changed nothing. I've thought about that far more often than I've thought about the traffic.
models.len: about 118 seconds — stopped by the examiner

notes.fc: Two short opposed clauses open the turn and set a rhythm before any content arrives. The four prompts are all answered and none is visible as a prompt. The closing observation genuinely outlives the anecdote, and the pauses throughout are content-related rather than lexical.
notes.lr: Disposed of, impromptu village, strung out along the hard shoulder, more or less delighted. Idiomatic and precise, with a controlled shift into dry irony (on the theory that nobody else would be mad enough). The one-line paragraph People got out. carries weight through placement rather than vocabulary.
notes.gr: Conditional inversion (Had I been alone), past perfect continuous, a reduced participle clause, a fronted noun phrase, and an elliptical fragment used deliberately. Structures change with rhetorical function; errors are absent.
notes.pr: The opening two sentences demand contrastive stress on NINE and THREE. Not to look — to talk requires a mid-utterance break and a pitch reset. The final sentence slows and falls. Phonology is carrying meaning throughout, which is the Band 8 criterion stated exactly.

diffs: 118 seconds — stopped by the examiner, the ideal outcome
I want to talk about… — announces preparation
Two opposed clauses that set a rhythm before any content
Past perfect, past perfect continuous, sentential relative
Adds conditional inversion, participle clause, deliberate fragment
Specific and odd: sunflower seeds and phone chargers
A reflection on why it is remembered fondly
An observation about people that the story earned
Voice change in the quotation; one built pause
Pace varies by section; fragments and resets used structurally
